transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, I’m here because... I’m pretty sure the people on that environmental modeling contract have been tracking my revisions. They're planting errors in the datasets on purpose to make it look like I can’t lead the work. My wife keeps telling me it’s just version-control mistakes. The junior analysts say the exact same thing, but they don't see it. 

Version control... you know, back when I first took a few math and computer classes in college, we didn't have any of these fancy cloud systems. We used those big five-and-a-quarter-inch floppy disks. The ones that were actually floppy? I used to keep mine in a plastic shoebox under my bed because the dust in my dorm was just terrible. My roommate, Greg, he never dusted. He was a geology major, always bringing literal dirt into the room. Just rocks everywhere. But anyway, yeah, they’re definitely slipping bad data into my models now.
How long have you been noticing these beliefs about your data being tampered with—did this start recently, or has it been going on for months or longer?

Well, the absolute certainty that they are tracking my revisions... that they're planting those errors on purpose, that really locked in about two months ago. Right around the time I had to get the car inspected. 

It was a Tuesday, I remember, because I took it down to that garage on 4th street. The mechanic there, Frank, he’s been working on my cars since the late nineties. He told me my brake pads were wearing thin, which is just ridiculous because I barely drive anywhere these days except to the grocery store. I always go on Tuesdays to get the store brand peanut butter, you know, because the name brands put way too much sugar in it now. It’s like eating candy for breakfast. If you actually read the labels, it’s all high-fructose corn syrup and hydrogenated oils. I tried explaining that to the cashier, but she was just staring at her phone. Kids today can't even hold a conversation without a screen in their face. 

But anyway, yeah, it's been about two straight months of them messing with my project data.

Over these past two months, have you noticed any significant changes in your mood—like feeling unusually sad, hopeless, or on the other hand, unusually energetic, elated, or irritable—that lasted most of the day for several days at a time?

No, my mood has been fine, really. I haven't been sad or anything like that. I mean, maybe a little stressed, but who wouldn't be with all this going on? But no, my mood is pretty steady. 

I've always been pretty even-keeled, actually. Even back when I was working at the hardware store in my twenties. I used to mix paint, and you'd get these people coming in, absolutely furious because the shade of beige wasn't exactly what they pictured in their head. Beige! There are a hundred shades of beige. Navajo White, Antique White, Swiss Coffee... Swiss Coffee isn't even coffee colored, it's just white with a drop of yellow in it. I never understood why they named it that. I prefer a nice, solid blue myself. We painted our first apartment blue. Well, the bedroom anyway. The landlord was furious when we moved out, said we had to paint it back to white, but he kept the security deposit anyway. Landlords, they always find a way to keep your money, don't they? 

But anyway, no, my mood hasn't been unusually high or low or anything. Just normal.
Have you experienced anything unusual with your senses recently—like hearing voices, sounds, or seeing things that others around you don't seem to notice?

No, no voices or anything like that. My hearing is actually perfectly fine, though my wife insists I'm going deaf because I keep the TV volume turned up. But it's not my hearing, it's the way they mix the audio on television these days. The dialogue is just a whisper, and then suddenly the sound effects are completely deafening. 

I was trying to watch this program the other night about the Fibonacci sequence in nature—fascinating stuff, really, how pinecones and sunflowers follow the exact same mathematical spiral. You can model the growth patterns perfectly with just a simple recursive formula. But the background music was so incredibly loud I couldn't even hear the narrator. They use these heavy cellos for absolutely everything now. Every single program has to have this dramatic, moody cello music. 

My uncle Arthur played the cello, actually. He had to carry that giant heavy case everywhere he went. He drove this massive wood-paneled station wagon just to fit the thing in the back. The gas mileage on those old wagons was a complete joke, maybe eight miles to the gallon on the highway if you had a tailwind. You'd spend half your paycheck just driving to the grocery store and back. But anyway... what were we saying? Right, no, I don't hear any strange voices or see things that aren't there. Just regular sounds.

Have you had any recent head injuries, been diagnosed with any medical conditions like thyroid problems or neurological issues, or been using any substances or new medications around the time these beliefs started?

No, no head injuries. I haven't hit my head or anything. And my thyroid is fine, I don't take any medications, no drugs or anything like that. 

I did get a new pair of glasses recently, though. Bifocals. It took me forever to get used to them. You have to tilt your head just right to look at the screen, otherwise all the numbers start swimming together. It's terrible for your posture. I was reading this article about ergonomics, and how sitting at a desk all day is basically destroying our spines. Humans weren't meant to sit in office chairs for eight hours a day. We evolved to be hunter-gatherers, moving around, walking miles every day. 

My grandfather, he used to walk five miles to work at the textile mill, every single morning, rain or shine. And he lived to be ninety-two! Never had a back problem in his life. He always wore these heavy leather boots, the kind they just don't make anymore. Everything nowadays is made out of cheap synthetic materials that fall apart after six months. You buy a pair of shoes now, and the soles start peeling off before you've even broken them in. It's planned obsolescence, that's what it is. They want you to keep buying and buying. 

But no, to answer your question, my health is fine. No medical issues or new pills or anything like that.

Aside from the situation with your project data, has anything else in your daily life changed—like your ability to do your job, keep up with responsibilities at home, or spend time with friends and family?

Well, work has been... difficult. I’ve fallen pretty far behind on my modeling deliverables, actually. It got to the point where the firm had to reassign some pieces of my contract. I just couldn't concentrate on the data. And the junior analysts I'm supposed to be supervising, I haven't been much help to them lately either. 

Speaking of junior analysts, they hire them so young now, straight out of undergrad, and they don't even teach them proper Fortran anymore. It's all Python this and R that. I mean, Python is fine for quick scripting, but if you want real computational efficiency for large-scale matrix operations, you need a compiled language. I remember when we used to have to book time on the mainframe. You'd submit your punch cards and wait overnight for the results. If you made one syntax error, you lost twenty-four hours. It taught you discipline! You had to actually think through your algorithms before you ran them. 

Now they just throw computing power at everything. Brute force. Nobody optimizes their code anymore. It's like how they build houses these days, just slapping up drywall instead of taking the time to do proper plastering. My uncle—not Arthur with the cello, but my uncle Henry—he was a plasterer. Real craftsman. He could make a ceiling smooth as glass. Took him days, but it lasted fifty years. 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right, responsibilities. At home, I mostly just keep to myself these days. My wife has been having to push me quite a bit just to keep basic routines going, you know, getting up, eating... that sort of thing.

Aside from your worries about the project data, have you noticed a general loss of interest or motivation in things you used to enjoy, or a flattening of your emotions, even in situations unrelated to that concern?

Well, yeah, I suppose so. I just don't feel much pull to start anything or talk to anyone lately. I can just sit for hours at my desk, or out in the garage. The telescope is out there, still covered up. I used to love astronomy nights, taking the scope out to the dark sky preserve. 

The light pollution around here has gotten completely out of hand, though. You can barely see Orion on a clear winter night anymore. They put up those new LED streetlights in the neighborhood—the bright blue-white ones. They're absolutely terrible for your circadian rhythm. I was reading a study about how artificial light at night is disrupting the migration patterns of nocturnal birds. They get confused by the city lights and end up flying in circles until they drop from exhaustion. 

It's a tragedy, really, how disconnected we've become from the natural world. My father used to know the name of every bird that came to our feeder. He built this incredible wooden feeder out of cedar, hand-carved the edges. Cedar is fantastic wood, naturally rot-resistant. You don't even have to paint it, it just weathers to this beautiful silvery gray. You try buying a birdhouse now, it's all cheap plastic from overseas that cracks after one freeze. 

But, um, what were we talking about? Oh, right, interest in things. Yeah, I used to enjoy hiking too, and mentoring the younger analysts, like I said. But now... I just sit there. The telescope just stays covered. I just don't have the motivation for any of it anymore.

Before the data-tampering beliefs became fully certain two months ago, had you already been noticing yourself withdrawing, losing motivation, or having trouble concentrating for a longer stretch of time—say, going back four, five, or six months or more?

Well, no, it wasn't just four or five months ago. This whole... decline, or whatever you want to call it, it really started after I was put in charge of the larger environmental modeling contract. That was about two years and two months ago. 

That contract, it was massive. We were modeling groundwater dispersion across three counties. Groundwater is fascinating, really. It moves so slowly, inches a year in some aquifers. People think of it like underground rivers, but it's more like water soaking through a giant sponge made of rock and sand. The Ogallala Aquifer, out in the Great Plains? It's drying up. Farmers are pumping it out faster than the rain can replenish it. We're going to have a major agricultural crisis on our hands in a few decades if we don't change our irrigation practices. 

They use these center-pivot irrigators, you know, those huge metal arms on wheels that spray water in a circle? Terrible efficiency. Most of the water evaporates before it even hits the roots. Drip irrigation is the way to go. The Israelis perfected it back in the sixties. You run these little plastic tubes right along the crop lines and just drip the water exactly where it's needed. Saves a fortune in water costs. 

But I guess they don't want to invest the capital upfront. It's always about the short-term profits. Just like the modeling contract. They wanted results faster than the computation would allow, so I had to... well, I had to take charge of it. But yeah, that was about two years and two months ago when I really started pulling back from everything else.

You don't even have to paint it, it just weathers to this beautiful silvery gray. You try buying a birdhouse now, it's all cheap plastic from overseas that cracks after one freeze. 

But, um, what were we talking about? Oh, right, interest in things. Yeah, I used to enjoy hiking too, and mentoring the younger analysts, like I said. But now... I just sit there. The telescope just stays covered. I just don't have the motivation for any of it anymore.

inference.note: The presence of prominent negative symptoms (anhedonia, avolition, social withdrawal), disorganized/tangential speech pattern, and functional decline across multiple domains beyond the delusional theme are inconsistent with delusional disorder (F22), which requires preserved functioning and absence of other psychotic domain symptoms. This shifts the picture toward schizophrenia (F20.9), which under ICD-10 criteria only requires ~1 month of active symptoms.

doctor.intent: Determine total duration of continuous disturbance (including prodromal social withdrawal/negative symptoms) to assess whether it exceeds 6 months, which is key to differentiating schizophrenia from schizophreniform disorder or brief psychotic disorder.
doctor.question: Before the data-tampering beliefs became fully certain two months ago, had you already been noticing yourself withdrawing, losing motivation, or having trouble concentrating for a longer stretch of time—say, going back four, five, or six months or more?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the timeline of the symptoms, specifically how long the withdrawal, loss of motivation, or trouble concentrating had been happening before the data-tampering beliefs started (asking if it goes back four, five, or six months or more). This maps directly to the 'Duration' symptom profile, which states the decline started 2 years and 2 months ago.

patient.answer:
Well, no, it wasn't just four or five months ago. This whole... decline, or whatever you want to call it, it really started after I was put in charge of the larger environmental modeling contract. That was about two years and two months ago. 

That contract, it was massive. We were modeling groundwater dispersion across three counties. Groundwater is fascinating, really. It moves so slowly, inches a year in some aquifers. People think of it like underground rivers, but it's more like water soaking through a giant sponge made of rock and sand. The Ogallala Aquifer, out in the Great Plains? It's drying up. Farmers are pumping it out faster than the rain can replenish it. We're going to have a major agricultural crisis on our hands in a few decades if we don't change our irrigation practices. 

They use these center-pivot irrigators, you know, those huge metal arms on wheels that spray water in a circle? Terrible efficiency. Most of the water evaporates before it even hits the roots. Drip irrigation is the way to go. The Israelis perfected it back in the sixties. You run these little plastic tubes right along the crop lines and just drip the water exactly where it's needed. Saves a fortune in water costs. 

But I guess they don't want to invest the capital upfront. It's always about the short-term profits. Just like the modeling contract. They wanted results faster than the computation would allow, so I had to... well, I had to take charge of it. But yeah, that was about two years and two months ago when I really started pulling back from everything else.

inference.note: The two-year-plus duration of prodromal decline (social withdrawal, avolition, anhedonia, occupational decline) combined with persistent circumscribed persecutory delusions, tangential/circumstantial thought process, and absence of mood episode, hallucinations, or medical/substance cause continues to support schizophrenia. Mood symptoms and perceptual disturbances have been ruled out, and the chronicity argues against schizophreniform or brief psychotic disorder, and against delusional disorder alone given the prominent disorganized speech and negative symptoms.
